questions.def: Few means not many, implying surprise. A few means some.
questions.question: ___ students failed the exam, which was unexpected.

questions.def: Several means more than two but not many, countable nouns.
questions.question: I've read ___ interesting books this year.

questions.def: A number of is used with countable nouns.
questions.question: A ___ of people attended the conference.

questions.def: Little is used with uncountable nouns and means almost none.
questions.question: I have ___ money left, so we can't eat out.

questions.def: Some is used for uncountable nouns like information.
questions.question: ___ of the information was useful to me.

questions.def: Quantity refers to the amount of something, often uncountable.
questions.question: Only a small ___ of water remained.

questions.def: Most can be used before a noun without 'of' if unspecified.
questions.question: ___ of the books on the shelf are mine.

questions.def: More is used for uncountable nouns when expressing quantity.
questions.question: I need ___ time to finish this project.

questions.def: A number of is used with countable nouns and plural verbs.
questions.question: A large ___ of errors were found.

questions.def: Much is used with uncountable nouns like time.
questions.question: She spent ___ of her free time reading books.

questions.def: Sufficient describes an adequate amount of something uncountable.
questions.question: We have ___ information on the subject.

questions.def: Amount is used for uncountable nouns, like effort.
questions.question: A significant ___ of effort was required.

questions.def: Every piece emphasizes each individual portion.
questions.question: ___ of the cake was delicious.

questions.def: Numerous means a large number of, used with countable nouns.
questions.question: There are ___ ways to solve this problem.

questions.def: Number is used with countable nouns, tickets.
questions.question: A limited ___ of tickets are available.

questions.def: Some is used to indicate a portion of a group.
questions.question: ___ of my friends are coming to the party.

questions.def: Any is used in negative sentences and questions.
questions.question: I don't have ___ information about that.

questions.def: Amount is used for uncountable nouns, like resources.
questions.question: An insufficient ___ of resources led to failure.

questions.def: Several refers to a number greater than two, countable nouns.
questions.question: ___ of the employees received a bonus.

questions.def: Considerable means a large amount of, uncountable noun.
questions.question: She has ___ experience in this field.

questions.def: Many is used with countable nouns like people.
questions.question: Much people attended the event yesterday.

questions.def: Few is used with countable nouns, participants.
questions.question: Only a ___ of participants registered.

questions.def: Few (without 'a') suggests a lack of friends.
questions.question: He has ___ friends, which makes him lonely.

questions.def: Plenty of means a large amount of; uncountable nouns.
questions.question: I have ___ work to do today.

questions.def: 'A few' means some, enough to matter. 'Few' means almost none.
questions.question: ___ students attended the lecture yesterday.

questions.def: 'All' needs 'the' before a specific noun phrase.
questions.question: All ___ information will be kept confidential.

questions.def: 'Number' is correct with countable nouns like 'people'.
questions.question: A ___ of people complained about the service.

questions.def: 'Enough' describes the quantity of uncountable nouns.
questions.question: There isn't ___ evidence to support his claim.

questions.def: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'time'.
questions.question: He devoted ___ of his time to charity.

questions.def: 'Little' implies almost no hope in this context.
questions.question: There is ___ hope that the situation will improve.
